summary:
Our analysis of your current database architecture reveals two highly viable modernization paths, with DynamoDB emerging as the optimal choice for both cost efficiency and performance optimization. After analyzing 6 source tables handling 893 requests per second across 5 primary query groups, DynamoDB demonstrates an 82% confidence score with projected monthly costs of $33.37, representing a 88% cost reduction compared to DocumentDB's $272.20 alternative. The migration complexity is assessed as medium for both platforms, with all 6 tables showing high or suitable compatibility for DynamoDB migration, while only minimal anti-patterns were detected that can be addressed through complementary services like OpenSearch for full-text search capabilities.

The recommended DynamoDB architecture leverages strategic denormalization and item collections to eliminate expensive multi-table JOINs that currently impact your discussion detail pages and tag lookup operations. Key optimizations include consolidating discussions, posts, and tags into item collections that enable single-partition queries, and implementing a sharded Global Secondary Index (GSI) for the DiscussionsByLastPost access pattern to distribute the 192 write capacity units per second across 10 partitions. These design decisions directly address your highest-traffic query groups, particularly the Discussion reads (246 rps) and Discussion writes (196 rps), while maintaining your 10ms service level objectives through single GetItem and Query operations.

The migration presents manageable trade-offs that align with your application's usage patterns. User information denormalization will require fan-out updates via DynamoDB Streams when users modify their profiles, but with an average of 43 discussions and 126 posts per user across 500 users, this represents a controlled update volume. Similarly, tag name denormalization eliminates the 12,863 requests per second currently required for tag lookups, with minimal risk given your stable set of 5 tags. The primary technical risks are rated as low to medium and include implementing OpenSearch integration for full-text search and replacing database views with application-layer aggregation logic, both of which are standard patterns in modern cloud-native architectures.
summary_deterministic: Analyzed 6 source tables and 28 query patterns across 3 target database(s). Top recommendation: dynamodb with 82% average confidence. Schema design produced 3 target tables with 26 access patterns across 9 query groups. 6 source tables mapped to dynamodb. Estimated monthly cost: $305.57. 3 risk(s) identified (overall: LOW). Top query groups by throughput: Discussion reads, Discussion writes, Post writes. Other targets evaluated: documentdb (81%), elasticache (0%).

risks.description: [documentdb] trigger: trg_records_set_updated_at — DocumentDB does not support triggers. The application layer must set the 'updated_at' field to the current ISODate on every updateOne/updateMany call. Wrap this logic in a shared data-access helper or repository method to guarantee consistency across all write paths.

trade_offs: Item collection (discussions + posts + tags): Gained single-partition Query for discussion detail page (discussion + all posts) and eliminated 3-table JOIN for tag lookup. Traded independent scaling of posts — a viral discussion with thousands of posts could grow the item collection, but at ~2.9 posts/discussion avg this is well within DynamoDB 10 GB partition limit.

User username and email denormalized into DISCUSSION and POST items: Gained single GetItem/Query for discussion/post detail with author info (eliminates JOIN, meets 10ms SLO). Traded write amplification when a user updates email/username — all their discussions and posts must be updated. At 500 users and ~43 discussions + ~126 posts per user, a fan-out update via DynamoDB Streams + Lambda is manageable.

Tag name denormalized from tags reference table into TAG entity items: Gained DiscussionsByTag GSI query on tag_name directly, eliminating the 3-table JOIN (12,863 FTS). Traded update complexity if a tag is renamed — all ~6,441 TAG items per tag must be updated. With only 5 tags that rarely change, this is acceptable.

DiscussionsByLastPost GSI PK sharded into 10 partitions (DISC#0 through DISC#9): Gained write distribution for the mutable last_post_at sort key (192 WCU/s total -> 19.2 per shard). Traded read complexity — listing recent discussions requires scatter-gather across 10 shards and client-side merge-sort. Application must issue 10 parallel Query calls and merge-sort results.

Upvote uniqueness enforced via PutItem ConditionExpression attribute_not_exists(user_id) instead of dedicated lookup tables: Gained simple single-item write (1 WCU). The composite PK(user_id) + SK(DISC#id / POST#id) naturally enforces both unique constraints. No TransactWriteItems needed.

Username uniqueness on Users table enforced at the application layer. Email lookup served by UsersByEmail GSI (KEYS_ONLY). No query pattern was observed for username-based lookup. If strict database-level username uniqueness is required, a dedicated UsernameLookup table with TransactWriteItems can be added.

Discussion counter updates (post_count, upvote_count) use DynamoDB atomic ADD expressions: Gained contention-free increments eliminating MySQL row-level lock contention (37% lock_time_pct, 2,716 errors on post_count; 9.9% lock_time_pct, 1,352 errors on upvote_count). Traded strict transactional consistency — counter and upvote record are not atomically linked. Eventual consistency is acceptable for display counters.

Post upvote_count updates (AP-16, AP-26) require the application to supply discussion_id alongside post_id to construct the composite key: Gained item-collection co-location of posts with discussions. Traded application complexity — the app must track discussion context and the full composite SK (POST#<created_at>#<post_id>) from the initial post query. This is natural in the forum UI where posts are always viewed within a discussion.

TAG entity items store denormalized last_post_at, title, and post_count from parent discussion for DiscussionsByTag GSI projection: Gained single GSI query returning all display fields. Traded write amplification — when discussion last_post_at or post_count changes, all TAG items (~1.5 per discussion) must also be updated. At ~96 RPS * 1.5 tags = ~144 additional WCU/s, manageable.

UsersByEmail GSI has no mapped access pattern among the 26 documented patterns. This is likely an authentication flow (login by email) not captured in the MySQL performance_schema slow query log. Kept because KEYS_ONLY on 500 items has negligible cost and email-based lookup is a standard auth requirement.

[PE note] DISCUSSION entity definition is missing 3 attributes that are critical for the design to function: (1) gsi_partition — the computed shard key (e.g., DISC#{id%10}) that powers the DiscussionsByLastPost GSI, (2) last_post_at — used as SK for the same GSI and updated by AP-3, (3) upvote_count — projected into DiscussionsByLastPost and updated by AP-12/AP-20. An ETL pipeline implementing this contract would produce incomplete items. Add these to the entity attribute list with appropriate source mappings or calculation definitions.

[PE note] DiscussionsByLastPost GSI projects user_email. Forum listing pages (AP-9, AP-18) rarely display author emails publicly. Consider removing user_email from the projection to reduce GSI item size (~12% smaller) and eliminate one write-amplification vector on email changes. If the application does need email on listing pages, document the reason.

[PE note] The hot partition analysis treats total table throughput as single-partition load, which is overly conservative for high-cardinality PKs like discussion_id. At ~21K discussions, the true per-partition write load is ~0.02 WCU/s, not 411.2 WCU/s. This doesn't affect the design but may cause unnecessary alarm during capacity reviews. Consider adding a note about effective per-partition load based on PK cardinality.

[documentdb] Single-table source maps 1:1 to a single 'records' collection with no embedding or referencing decisions required. This is the simplest migration topology and avoids any $lookup overhead.

[documentdb] JSON/JSONB 'metadata' column is stored as a native BSON sub-document, enabling dot-notation queries (e.g., {'metadata.source': 'web'}). Any frequently-queried nested field should have a dedicated index added post-migration based on observed workload.

[documentdb] The source database trigger for 'updated_at' auto-stamping is replaced by application-layer logic. This trades server-enforced consistency for application-layer responsibility; all write paths must be audited to ensure the timestamp is always set.

[documentdb] The summary view (vw_records_status_summary) is replaced by a runtime aggregation pipeline. For low-frequency dashboard reads this is acceptable; if calls_per_second exceeds SLO thresholds, pre-materialization via a 'stats' collection with Change Streams should be implemented.
[documentdb] Unique index on 'email' preserves the RDBMS uniqueness constraint at slight write-overhead cost but is essential for data integrity during and after migration.
[documentdb] Document sizes are well within the 16 MB limit (estimated max ~4 KB). No sharding or document-splitting strategies are needed for the foreseeable growth horizon.

[documentdb] [PE note] The 'metadata' sub-document has a variable shape across documents (different keys per record). Post-migration, monitor query patterns against metadata fields — if any dot-notation query (e.g., {'metadata.source': 'web'}) becomes frequent, add a targeted single-field index. Do NOT use a wildcard index ($**) as it is unsupported in DocumentDB.

[documentdb] [PE note] AP-7's full collection scan for status counts is fine at low volume. If this dashboard query exceeds ~1 call/sec or the collection grows past ~1M documents, implement the pre-materialized 'stats' collection strategy described in the migration notes. Change Streams are available in DocumentDB 4.0+ for this purpose.

[documentdb] [PE note] The application-layer responsibility for setting 'updated_at' is a known risk. Consider adding a integration/contract test that verifies every write path through the repository layer sets updated_at, to prevent regression.

[documentdb] [PE note] Integer _id values are used (1001, 1002, 1003). Confirm the migration will preserve these as the original integer type rather than converting to ObjectId. If using auto-incrementing IDs, the application layer will need a sequence generator since DocumentDB does not have native auto-increment — alternatively, switch to ObjectId for new records post-migration.
